source.title: Scaling Verification Can Be More Effective than Scaling Policy Learning for Vision-Language-Action Alignment
source.authors: Jacky Kwok; Xilun Zhang; Mengdi Xu; Yuejiang Liu; Azalia Mirhoseini; Chelsea Finn; Marco Pavone

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests scaling of embodied action error and verifier accuracy, not held-out language-model pretraining loss, language-model extrapolation, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.gate_note: The paper reports power-law-like results for robot action error as action proposals or inference compute increase. These are related scaling results, but they are not the language-model loss or allocation measures named in the claim versions. Verifier retrieval-accuracy scaling and downstream robot success results are also outside those versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to robot oracle action error against the number of test-time action candidates. It also shows verifier retrieval accuracy rising with verifier size, data, batch size, epochs and ensemble size. None of these is held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens or training compute, in language or any other modality. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that allocating deployment compute to reasoning and verification can beat scaling policy training alone. Their evidence is gains on SIMPLER (+22% in-distribution, +13% out-of-distribution versus scaling policy pre-training on the same data), PolaRiS (+14% task progress, +9% success) and real-world tasks (+45%).
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates embodied test-time action sampling and a contrastive robot-action verifier, not the language-model pretraining scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The action-error scaling results vary with sampling strategy; the paper reports different fitted exponents for Gaussian perturbation, repeated sampling, instruction rephrasing, and hybrid sampling.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle best-of-k action error falls with the number of test-time action candidates. The fitted log-log slope depends on the sampling strategy: b from -0.12 (Gaussian perturbation) to -0.30 (hybrid sampling).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time (inference) scaling: oracle error falls as a power law in sample count, with an exponent set by sample diversity.

fits_no_version.finding: With CoVer selecting among VLA action candidates, selected-action RMSE falls from 0.166 at N=1 to 0.147 at N=16, and the gains flatten.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verifier-selected best-of-N lowers robot action error with diminishing returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Verifier top-1 retrieval accuracy rises monotonically with parameters (250M to 1B), synthetic instructions (8x to 64x), batch size, epochs and ensemble size (Figure 6). No power-law fit is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive VLA verifier accuracy improves with model size, data and compute.

record.problems: The reported action-error scaling concerns embodied action proposals rather than language-model held-out loss. Figure 3 gives aggregate errors and fitted parameters but does not provide uncertainty definitions or detailed fit diagnostics in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Verifier top-1 retrieval-accuracy scaling, downstream robot success rates, and latency measurements were not included because they do not measure the loss or allocation outcomes named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; no language-model training runs.
Extrapolation from small to large training runs.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities. Verifier scaling is reported only as top-1 retrieval accuracy, with no loss and no power-law fit, so it is not V5.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of training-scaling exponents on fitting choices.

missing.what: Verifier scaling curves for top-1 retrieval accuracy against model size, dataset size, batch size, epochs and ensemble size. These bear on no version, but the rows omit them.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling law' only in the test-time inference sense. It applies C≈6ND as a FLOP estimate but does not test any training scaling law.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model training runs predict much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter and token allocation under a fixed language-model training compute budget.
Architecture-shape effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream language-model task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: robot policy π(a | s, I)
rows.operation_detail: Repeatedly sample actions and measure oracle action error as candidate count increases.

conditions.value: 1,000 (s, a, I) tuples uniformly sampled from Bridge V2

rows.measure: Oracle action error; fitted power-law parameters a and b for log(error) versus log(candidate count)
rows.note: The paper describes oracle action error as decreasing with candidate count; this is an embodied action-error result, not language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: The value 'Error: 0.0024 ± 0.0024' in the Figure 3 legend is most likely a fit-residual statistic, not the oracle action error itself. The plotted errors are about 0.02–0.18. The row should record the fitted exponent b=-0.12 with that caveat.

source_check.correct: Gaussian perturbation: a=0.16, b=-0.12 in log(e)≈log(a)+b·log(k). The legend separately reports Error: 0.0024 ± 0.0024 without defining that statistic; it is not identified as oracle action error at a specified candidate count.
source_check.problem: The row presents an undefined legend error statistic as measured oracle action error and its uncertainty.

rows.subject: VLA policy (model not specified)
rows.operation_detail: Greedy decoding with one action candidate; measure selected-action RMSE.

relation.reason: The paper discusses scaling and training-versus-inference compute allocation, but its own power-law analysis measures a different construct from the specified claim versions.

tranche.reason: The fitted power laws concern oracle robot-action error versus inference-time candidate count or compute. Verifier-training ablations report retrieval-accuracy improvements without testing the catalog's training-loss power laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture invariance, or downstream predictability laws.

source_check.notes: Figure 3 uses NRMSE with an oracle, whereas Table 6 uses RMSE after CoVer selection. The Figure 3 legend does not define its separate Error statistic; interpreting it as fit residuals remains an inference.
